searchPolicy: Rate-limited Commons title search plus geotag and dive-site-name searches for named dive sites within each area; optional Openverse searches query large photos under accepted open licenses. A photo can show underwater life, coastline, wildlife, or a scenic land or cityscape. A geotag within 10 km of a named dive site, an exact area-name phrase, a named dive-site phrase, or an Openverse title/source tag matching a named area component can establish place even when scene wording is sparse; generic or homonymous place names require a second local phrase. Clear off-topic subjects remain excluded. Description-only matches still need scenic or destination context. Candidates must pass minimum-dimension, aesthetic-proxy, accepted-license, attribution, and explicit AI-generation-marker checks. Underwater and coastal scenes receive a ranking preference. Each image content hash or source page is assigned at most once.
selectionNote: Unmatched areas have no photo. Geotagged files within 10 km of a named dive site, exact area or dive-site title phrases, and Openverse results whose title or human-applied source tags name a place component can qualify despite sparse scene descriptions. Generic and homonymous names need additional local context. Description-only matches still need scenic context. Visual beauty and exact subject relevance need human review. The aesthetic score favors Commons-curated image categories, high resolution, and strong landscape framing; it is a shortlist signal, not a guarantee of beauty. Automated picks remain unreviewed until a person inspects each image. Absence of an AI-generation marker is not proof a file was human-made.

entries.label: Saint Pierre and Miquelon
entries.matchEvidence: Exact area name occurs in the Commons file title; this supplies place evidence even when scene wording is sparse.
entries.alt: Saint Pierre and Miquelon is a French archipelago south of the Canadian island of Newfoundland. Sparsely populated Miquelon--Langlade island contains the Grand Barachois lagoon, home to seabirds and seals. The busier Saint Pierre island has a distinct French atmosphere, with a cathedral and the Musée Heritage, which celebrates regional history. An island nearby, Île-aux-Marins, features an abandoned fishing village. Population is 6,000 and they use the Euro. Most of the population is employed by the French Government

entries.alt: We were up near Victoria, BC for a gardening conference this weekend. I skipped out Saturday afternoon and went for a hike in Gowlland Tod Provincial Park up to Holmes Peak and Jocelyn Hill via the Ridgetop Trail. One challenge was more than 20 cm of snow, which is quite unusual in the Victoria area. It was a fun hike, I saw lots of my favorite trees Arbutus menziesii . I made it up to near the top of Jocelyn Hill when the weather turned sour and I decided it was time to head back to Sidney for some scones and book shopping. Thanks to Flickr member Calypso Orchid for giving me some great Saanich Peninsula hiking tips, I have to come try a springtime hike up here. Update 7 March 2015 Arbutus menziesii has been disappearing in the Pacific Northwest, see The Decline of the Pacific Madrone vi 018

entries.alt: We attended the Vancouver Island Rock and Alpine Garden Society 2011 Western Winter Study Weekend in Sidney, BC from 25 to 27 February. The theme was Plants Along the Silk Road. I attended talks Friday night by Dr. Bobby J. Ward Modern-Day Plant Hunters and Hans Roemer on The Silk Road through the Wakhan Corridor, Afghanistan Saturday I heard Vojtěch Holubec on The Celestial Mountains - Tien Shan Alpines and bulbs from Uzbekistan, Kazakstan and Kyrgystan and Bill Terry on Poppies along the Silk Road (I then skipped out in order to go hiking and then book shopping in Sidney....) Saturday night we had a fun banquet followed by a nice multimedia show by Yvonne Rorison: Images from Far and Near to Capture the Imagination Sunday morning I listened to Stephanie Ferguson talk about garden design and plant selection for her Calgary rock garden - Sun, Stone and Water: Growing Exquisite Plants from Remote Alpine and Steppe-Desert Environments. (Skipped out again for more book shopping...) Finally, I attended another interesting talk by Vojtěch Holubec on Pamir and Donkeys: How donkeys are important in plant hunting vi 010 Corydalis is Zygomorphic. Zygomorphic ("yoke shaped", "bilateral") flowers can be divided by only a single plane into two mirror-image halves, much like a yoke or a person's face. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floral_symmetry#Zygomorphic

entries.alt: The Belize Barrier Reef is one of the most significant reef systems in the Western Hemisphere, celebrated for its exceptional marine biodiversity and striking natural formations. Its coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrass beds support a wide range of species, including several that are threatened or endangered. The site also showcases important ecological processes that sustain the wider Caribbean marine environment. UNESCO recognizes the reef for its outstanding natural value and its crucial role in global conservation efforts.

entries.alt: The Sea Cadet Corps training facility "TS Venture" , on Ireland Island , the historical core of the Royal Navy facilities in the Imperial fortress colony of Bermuda , and the location of the Royal Naval Dockyard . The building, which is located to the south of the Royal Naval Cemetery and to the north of the former site of the Royal Naval Hospital, Bermuda, was constructed by dockyard artisans in 1857 as a an Ancient Order of Foresters Friendly Society hall, and was later a Catholic chapel (there was also a Church of England chapel in the dockyard, and a Methodist chapel on the northern side the Royal Naval Cemetery. The Corps has three units in Bermuda, all on former naval properties, and collectively the three operate as the Bermuda Sea Cadet Corps , though part of the larger British Corps.

entries.alt: View from the ferry to Orcas Island. If I have my geography right, Orcas Island is on the left side, Blakely Island on the right, and Obstruction Island in between. Behind Obstruction Island is Lummi Island's Lummi Peak, I think. The strait on the left (north) side of Obstruction Island is Obstruction Pass, while the one on the right (south) is Peavine Pass (mostly hidden from this angle). The giant glacier-covered volcano is Mt Baker, and the line of jagged high ridges to the right is, I think, Twin Sisters Mountain.

entries.alt: King angelfish ( Holacanthus passer ), Cabo Pulmo, Baja California, Mexico. The king angelfish is a non-migratory tropical fish that inhabits reefs in the eastern Pacific Ocean from the coast of Peru north to the Gulf of California, generally at depth of 4–30 metres (13–98 ft). Adult king angelfish are generally about 35 centimetres (1.15 ft) in length. They are diurnal and feed on sponges, other sessile invertebrates, zooplankton, and certain species of benthic microalgae.

entries.alt: This is another lighthouse for my book I did not have. Someday I may get to the island for a closer view. Coffin Island light was the first lighthouse built in Liverpool Bay in 1812. The fifth lighthouse in Nova Scotia, built of wood, the octagonal building stood 22.9 meter (75ft) high. It had the latest in technology, the first revolving light in Nova Scotia. Known as a catoptric light, the clockwork mechanism turned fourteen Argand lamps and parabolic reflectors. Revolving every two minutes, the light could be seen up to 15 miles away. The lighthouse was struck by lightning on June 19, 1913 and the fire destroyed it and all of the outbuildings. A year later (1914) a 15.8 meter (52ft) steel reinforced concrete lighthouse was completed. In 2006 the Department of Fisheries and Oceans replaced the second lighthouse built in 1914 with a fibreglass lighthouse. Another one for my book (free to view) www.blurb.com/books/9075431-eastern-canadian-lighthouses-...

entries.alt: Coiba separated from continental Panama about 12,000 to 18,000 years ago when sea levels rose. entries.alt: Retiro Park is the most beautiful park in Madrid. Here are beautiful walking paths and there are boats for rent on the central lake. The Retiro is Madrid's best known park. It occupies 120 hectares of land in the very center of the city. It originated as the gardens of the Palace of the Buen Retiro and was opened to the public by decree of the First Spanish Republic in 1868. The Retiro includes the Rosaleda (a rose garden) and a boating lake, around which there is always a large variety of shows and street theatre during the weekends.

This picture was created by my fearless friend epSos.de and can be used for free, if you link epSos.de as the original author of the image. The height of the cliff in this image is about 15 meters to the surface of the sea waves. The cold water, the salty ocean depth and the risk of falling made the white shoes to tremble on the shaking feet that were struggling to keep the legs in a safe position. The dangerous rocks of the yellow mountain made it a perfect location of an unplanned fall. If such a fall would occur someone might think it would be a suicide. In reality this picture was created to demonstrate the suicidal danger of playing with the adrenaline by overcoming natural fears of heights. Thank you for sharing this picture with your friends !

entries.alt: Lake Erie is the fourth largest lake (by surface area) of the five Great Lakes in North America, and the thirteenth largest globally if measured in terms of surface area. It is the southernmost, shallowest, and smallest by volume of the Great Lakes and therefore also has the shortest average water residence time. At its deepest point Lake Erie is 210 feet (64 metres) deep. Lake Erie's northern shore is bounded by the Canadian province of Ontario, with US states of Ohio, Pennsylvania and New York on its southern and easternmost shores and Michigan on the west. These jurisdictions divide the surface area of the lake by water boundaries. The lake was named by the Erie tribe of Native Americans who lived along its southern shore. That Iroquoian tribe called it "Erige" ("cat") because of its unpredictable and sometimes violently dangerous nature. It is a matter of conjecture whether the lake was named after the tribe, or if the tribe was called "Erie" because of its proximity to the lake. Situated below Lake Huron, Erie's primary inlet is the Detroit River. The main natural outflow from the lake is via the Niagara River, which provides hydroelectric power to Canada and the U.S. as it spins huge turbines near Niagara Falls at Lewiston, New York and Queenston, Ontario. Some outflow occurs via the Welland Canal which diverts water for ship passages from Port Colborne, Ontario on Lake Erie, to St. Catharines on Lake Ontario, an elevation difference of 326 ft (99 m). Lake Erie's environmental health has been an ongoing concern for decades, with issues such as overfishing, pollution and algae blooms and eutrophication generating headlines. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Erie en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Text_of_Creative_Commons_...

entries.alt: Found at the Red River Refuge in Bossier City, LA. This was a really neat find. Eumesosoma is a member of the suborder Eupnoi, and these types of harvestmen are commonly found in temperate regions of North America and Eurasia. Vonones ornata, however, is a cosmetid of the suborder Laniatores. Laniatorids (laniatorans?) are more tropically distributed compared to Eupnoi, and cosmetids follow this trend as well, with the genus Vonones being the sole representative of the family in the US. For context, Cosmetidae is the second most diverse family of harvestmen and is endemic to the New World, primarily in Central and South America, where in some regions they make up roughly one third to one half of all harvestmen species found (Pinto-da-Rocha, et al. 2007). So here we have two very distantly related harvestmen species with very different morphologies occupying a similar ecological niche: cryptically living under dead logs near moist, littoral areas of the southeast US. Why is this neat? Surely such converges happen all the time. What's cool it that Vonones carries with it the evolutionary history of a tropical lineage, with it's peculiar morphological adaptations and color patterns evolved for complex systems of defensive interactions and sexual communication, while Eumesosoma is comparatively rather bland looking, and has a different history in which Vonones' adaptations would have been superfluous in it's simpler temperate ecosystem. Not that Eumesosoma doesn't have it's own amazing peculiarities, it's just not wearing them on it's sleeve, so to speak. I must admit, however, that the association you see here isn't quite natural. I originally overturned this log and found the sclerosomatid only. However, after he tried to escape, and after rolling the log back and forth a number of times to keep him visible, all of a sudden two cosmetids appeared. Were they there on the log the whole time, simply evading my sight while I was paying attention the grey harvestman, or did they hop on at some later point? I have no clue. The trio did tolerate each other for some time before scattering (during which one of the cosmetids walked on top of the sclerosomatid, neither of which seemed to mind), although they were likely only trying to get out of the Sun, as they are negatively phototaxic, not necessarily trying to avoid each other. I often find V. ornata in pairs, and so their association wasn't surprising. I often find them next two isopods, ants, millipedes, and centipedes as well, but this was the first time I found them with another harvestmen species. A little later, I found a cosmetid next to a different eupnoian species, although not quite this close.

entries.alt: Lake Tahoe is a large freshwater lake in the Sierra Nevada of the United States. At a surface elevation of 6,225 ft (1,897 m), it is located along the border between California and Nevada, west of Carson City. Lake Tahoe is the largest alpine lake in North America. Its depth is 1,645 ft (501 m), making it the deepest in the United States after Crater Lake (1,945 ft (593 m)). Additionally, Lake Tahoe is the sixth largest lake by volume in the United States at 122,160,280 acre·ft (150,682,490 dam3), behind the five Great Lakes. The lake was formed about 2 million years ago and is a part of the Lake Tahoe Basin with the modern lake being shaped during the ice ages. It is known for the clarity of its water and the panorama of surrounding mountains on all sides. The area surrounding the lake is also referred to as Lake Tahoe, or simply Tahoe. More than 75% of the lake's watershed is national forest land, comprising the Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit of the United States Forest Service. Lake Tahoe is a major tourist attraction in both Nevada and California. It is home to a number of ski resorts, summer outdoor recreation, and tourist attractions. Snow and skiing are a significant part of the area's economy and reputation. Mountain and lake scenery are attractions throughout the year. The Nevada side also includes large casinos. Highways provide year-round access from Reno, Carson City, and Sacramento. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tahoe en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Text_of_Creative_Commons_...

entries.alt: U.S. Route 264 is an east–west United States highway that runs for 215.7 miles (347.1 km) from Raleigh to Manns Harbor, entirely in the U.S. state of North Carolina. U.S. Route 264 begins at the Raleigh Beltline (which carries US 64 and Interstate 440) and travels to the east from a directional T interchange, concurrently with US 64 along with it on a freeway alignment. It meets the eastern terminus of Interstate 540, which features several unused stub ramps. The route curves to the northeast, paralleling NC 97, until it passes by Zebulon. At the north side of town, US 64 continues to the northeast, while the US 264 freeway continues east through a long wooded stretch. It curves to the south just before it meets Interstate 95/Interstate 795, just west of Wilson. As the freeway loops south of Wilson, the short concurrency of Interstate 795 splits-off towards Goldsboro as US 264 continues east to Greenville. In Greenville, the freeway downgrades to expressway grade at the US 13/NC 11/NC 903 interchange. After completing the loop north around Greenville, it continues east, on Pactolus Highway, through a largely developed area and passes through Washington and US 17. The route continues east on a two-lane road, cutting through mostly farmland. It begins to curve to the northeast after meeting NC 99, entering Pantego on Main Street. Within the town, it curves to the east again and then south toward Belhaven, where it bypasses north of town while US 264 Business goes through it. After Belhaven, US 264 continues eastward once again entering Hyde county, passing south of Lake Mattamuskeet through an area dominated by farmland and through the community of Engelhard. Turning north, US 264 goes through the Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge before finally reaching Manns Harbor, where US 264 ends at intersection with US 64. Pamlico Scenic Byway is an 127-mile (204 km) byway from Washington to Manns Harbor. US 264 overlap several sections of the byway. The byway is noted for its history, scenic views, and the three national wildlife refuges that the route goes through. Other roads and highways that make-up the byway are: NC 32, NC 45, NC 92, and NC 94. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_264 en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Text_of_Creative_Commons_...

entries.alt: Beginning as a limestone quarry supplying limestone to a nearby cement plant in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania during much of the 20th Century, the industrial decline experienced by the rust belt during the 1960s and 1970s saw the closure of this former quarry in the mid-1970s, which subsequently flooded with a combination of storm runoff and groundwater. By 1980, the quarry had filled deep enough to make it a suitable scuba diving spot, with it opening to the public as Dutch Springs, operated by Stuart and Jane Wells Schooley, with an open water scuba diving facility, aqua park, and adventure course being located on the property around the quarry. The quarry operated until 2022, when the land was sold to a warehouse development, with the former owners being paid millions for the 95 acres of land so a development company could build two massive warehouses on the parts of the property not occupied by the quarry, with a proposal to fence the quarry off and leave it unused. However, due to the high-quality freshwater conditions in the quarry, a movement was started by divers in multiple parts of the Northeastern United States to prevent its closure. The movement succeeded in two local dive shop owners being donated the land by the developer, which will remain open for more limited open water scuba diving, under the name Lake Hydra. This photo was taken on Memorial Day Weekend in 2022, one of the last weekends Dutch Springs was open.

entries.alt: We attended the Vancouver Island Rock and Alpine Garden Society 2011 Western Winter Study Weekend in Sidney, BC from 25 to 27 February. The theme was Plants Along the Silk Road. I attended talks Friday night by Dr. Bobby J. Ward Modern-Day Plant Hunters and Hans Roemer on The Silk Road through the Wakhan Corridor, Afghanistan Saturday I heard Vojtěch Holubec on The Celestial Mountains - Tien Shan Alpines and bulbs from Uzbekistan, Kazakstan and Kyrgystan and Bill Terry on Poppies along the Silk Road (I then skipped out in order to go hiking and then book shopping in Sidney....) Saturday night we had a fun banquet followed by a nice multimedia show by Yvonne Rorison: Images from Far and Near to Capture the Imagination Sunday morning I listened to Stephanie Ferguson talk about garden design and plant selection for her Calgary rock garden - Sun, Stone and Water: Growing Exquisite Plants from Remote Alpine and Steppe-Desert Environments. (Skipped out again for more book shopping...) Finally, I attended another interesting talk by Vojtěch Holubec on Pamir and Donkeys: How donkeys are important in plant hunting vi 002

Saturday night we had a fun banquet followed by a nice multimedia show by Yvonne Rorison: Images from Far and Near to Capture the Imagination Sunday morning I listened to Stephanie Ferguson talk about garden design and plant selection for her Calgary rock garden - Sun, Stone and Water: Growing Exquisite Plants from Remote Alpine and Steppe-Desert Environments. (Skipped out again for more book shopping...) Finally, I attended another interesting talk by Vojtěch Holubec on Pamir and Donkeys: How donkeys are important in plant hunting vi 002

In the foreground and middle distance: Leblon, below, continuing toward Ipanema, with the apartment buildings and rooftops characteristic of the South Zone. On the left: Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas, with the buildings of the Lagoa and Fonte da Saudade neighbourhoods on the opposite shore and, behind them, the green, forested slopes of the massif. In the centre background: Morro do Cantagalo, the granite outcrop separating Ipanema from Copacabana. On its right-hand slope, the houses of the Cantagalo and Pavão-Pavãozinho favelas can be seen along the ridge. Copacabana is hidden behind this hill. On the right: Praia de Ipanema, the line of breaking waves and, in the background, Ponta do Arpoador closing off the beach, with its green rock beside the sea. In the far distance: the silhouettes of the hills near the entrance to Guanabara Bay, including Pão de Açúcar among the grey profiles on the left, and farther to the right, across the sea, the hills of Niterói’s oceanfront region with several small coastal islands.

entries.alt: O Forte de São Domingos da Baralha localiza-se entre o cabo Espichel e Sesimbra, no Distrito de Setúbal, em Portugal. Terá sido construído no Séc. XVII a mando de D. Afonso VI, contribuindo para a proteção e vigilância da costa. Foi destruído a 21 de junho de 1808 por um ataque de Inglaterra (aliados de Portugal contra os franceses) de forma a evitar que o forte fosse utilizado por França. São Domingos da Baralha Fort is located between Cape Espichel and Sesimbra, in the District of Setúbal, Portugal. It was built in the 17th century by order of the king D. Afonso VI, contributing to the protection and surveillance of the coast. It was destroyed on June 21, 1808 by an attack from England (Portugal's allies against the French) in order to prevent the fort from being used by France.

entries.alt: 221116-N-N3764-0304 SINT EUSTATIUS, Netherlands - (Nov. 16, 2022) – Sailors assigned to the Freedom-variant littoral combat ship USS Milwaukee (LCS 5) conduct a gun-salute for Statia Day off the coast of Sint Eustatius, Netherlands, Nov. 16, 2022. Statia Day is a national holiday celebrated on the Caribbean island of Sint Eustatius. It celebrates the “first salute” when Sint Eustatius, locally known as Statia, became the first country to recognize the United States as a nation 245 years ago when after the U.S. declared independence, a Continental Navy ship fired a gun salute upon entering the harbor, and the island, by order of the Dutch governor, returned the salute. Milwaukee is deployed to the U.S. 4th Fleet area of operations to support Joint Interagency Task Force South’s mission, which includes counter-illicit drug trafficking missions in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific. (U.S. Navy photo by Gunner’s Mate Seaman Hanna Westbrook/Released)

entries.alt: Ia Orana! I took my first real vacation in 3 years, deciding to turn 50 in beautiful Tahiti. I stayed in Papeete on the island of Tahiti, but also spent my birthday in an over-water bungalow in Huahine, and also spent a day on Moorea. Thanks to my host family (maruuru!), I got to visit many cultural and natural sights, tried a lot of native food, and despite spending the week sweating, had a wonderful time, living as both a tourist and native. French Polynesia, an overseas collectivity of France, comprises more than 100 islands in the South Pacific, stretching for more than 2,000km. Divided into the Austral, Gambier, Marquesas, Society and Tuamotu archipelagos, they're known for their coral-fringed lagoons and over-the-water bungalow hotels. Island features include white- and black-sand beaches, mountains, rugged backcountry and towering waterfalls.
